title: Shoulder Dystocia
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Shoulder dystocia is a delivery emergency where the fetal shoulders fail to deliver after the head, most often the anterior shoulder is impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis. Prompt recognition and a stepwise manoeuvre sequence are essential to prevent birth‑related trauma.

sections.p: Failure of the fetal shoulders to deliver within 1–2 minutes after the head has emerged, usually because the anterior shoulder is lodged behind the maternal pubic symphysis.
b: Turtle sign – the delivered head retracts toward the perineum
No restitution of the shoulders after gentle traction

sections.p: Severity is graded by the number and difficulty of manoeuvres required and by neonatal outcome.
b: Mild: resolved with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure only
Moderate: requires internal rotation (Wood’s screw, reverse‑rocker‑bottom) or delivery of the posterior arm
Severe: multiple manoeuvres, prolonged delivery (>5 min), or neonatal injury (brachial plexus palsy, fracture)

sections.p: Obstetric and fetal factors that increase shoulder width or reduce maternal pelvic capacity.
b: Fetal macrosomia (>4.5 kg) – most common
Maternal diabetes (gestational or pre‑existing)
Obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m²)
Previous shoulder dystocia
Post‑term pregnancy
Prolonged second stage (> 3 h nulliparous, > 2 h multiparous)
Instrumental delivery (forceps or vacuum)
Maternal pelvic floor rigidity

sections.p: During the second stage the head is delivered, then retracts; the shoulders do not follow despite gentle traction.
b: Turtle sign
Absence of the normal ‘shoulder‑to‑shoulder’ feel on bimanual exam
Maternal distress or excessive pushing without progress

t.b: Is the baby likely >4.5 kg? – predicts risk, guides preparation
Detects undiagnosed diabetes – allows tighter glycaemic control in future pregnancies
Confirms shoulder impaction and guides manoeuvre choice

t.a: Neonatal assessment (Apgar, tone, brachial plexus exam)
t.b: Identifies immediate injury; if unavailable, observe for lack of movement in upper limbs

sections.p: Complications arise from prolonged compression of the brachial plexus, clavicle, or humerus, and from maternal soft‑tissue injury.
b: Brachial plexus palsy (Erb’s or Klumpke)
Clavicular or humeral fracture
Maternal postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony after vigorous manoeuvres
Fetal hypoxia if delivery exceeds 5 min

sections.p: A rapid, coordinated response with a clear algorithm saves both mother and baby.
b: Call for help immediately – at least one additional skilled birth attendant and a senior obstetrician
McRoberts manoeuvre – hyperflex the mother’s thighs to the abdomen, relieving pelvic angle
Suprapubic pressure – firm pressure just above the pubic bone directed posteriorly
If unresolved: internal rotation (Wood’s screw), reverse‑rocker‑bottom, or delivery of the posterior arm
Avoid fundal pressure – increases risk of uterine rupture and fetal injury
Episiotomy only for clear indication (e.g., rigid perineum, fetal distress)
Post‑delivery: assess neonate for brachial plexus injury, fractures, and hypoxia; give oxygen and monitor vitals

sections.p: After an episode, both mother and infant need targeted review and future pregnancies require risk mitigation.
b: Neonatal follow‑up for brachial plexus recovery (physiotherapy if needed)
Maternal counselling on weight control, optimal glycaemic control, and birth spacing
Consider elective cesarean for subsequent pregnancies if risk factors persist (e.g., prior dystocia, estimated fetal weight >4.5 kg)
Audit of each case to improve team response

sections.p: Conditions that also cause difficulty delivering the shoulders or present with a retracted head.
b: Cephalopelvic disproportion – head fails to descend, not shoulders
Maternal uterine rupture – sudden loss of fetal station with abdominal pain
Fetal malpresentation (breech, transverse) – different delivery sequence

sections.p: Certain assessments may give false reassurance.
b: Clinical estimate of fetal weight can underestimate macrosomia, especially in obese mothers
Normal maternal glucose screen in early pregnancy does not rule out later gestational diabetes

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent turtle sign after 1 minute of attempts
Failure to deliver shoulders after 2 minutes of coordinated manoeuvres
Any sign of fetal distress (bradycardia, poor tone) during the emergency

faq.a: It can push the fetal head back into the pelvis, worsening shoulder impaction and increasing risk of uterine rupture.

faq.q: What is the first manoeuvre and why does it work?
faq.a: McRoberts – flexing the thighs flattens the sacrum and widens the pelvic outlet, often freeing the impacted shoulder.

faq.q: When is an episiotomy indicated in shoulder dystocia?
faq.a: Only if the perineum is rigid or if additional space is needed for manoeuvres; routine episiotomy offers no benefit.

exam: What is the ‘turtle sign’ and what does it tell you? — It is the retraction of the delivered head toward the perineum, indicating shoulder dystocia and prompting immediate manoeuvres.
List the first three steps you would take when shoulder dystocia is identified. — Call for help, perform McRoberts, apply suprapubic pressure; explain the rationale for each.

A mother with gestational diabetes delivers a 4.8 kg baby and you encounter a turtle sign. Which risk factor most likely contributed and how could it be mitigated in future pregnancies? — Maternal hyperglycaemia leads to fetal macrosomia; tight glucose control and possible elective cesarean reduce recurrence.
Why is Wood’s screw manoeuvre used only after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail? — It rotates the anterior shoulder internally, requiring more skill and time; earlier simpler measures are safer.

A newborn shows absent movement of the right arm after a difficult delivery. What injury should you suspect and what is the immediate management? — Erb’s palsy (upper brachial plexus); immobilise the arm, arrange physiotherapy, and monitor for spontaneous recovery.

During a shoulder dystocia, you notice the mother’s uterus is becoming atonic. What is your next step? — Treat uterine atony with uterine massage and oxytocin (if available) while continuing delivery manoeuvres.

How would you modify your management if suprapubic pressure is unavailable (e.g., no assistant to apply it)? — Increase the degree of McRoberts, consider early internal rotation or posterior arm delivery; ensure rapid escalation to senior help.
Explain why a prolonged second stage (>3 h) is a risk factor for shoulder dystocia. — Exhausted maternal muscles and fetal descent fatigue increase the chance of the shoulders becoming impacted.
